forces: Mixed chorus, baritone solo, orchestra and organ
performers: Bernard Kruysen, baritone; Chorale Philippe Caillard; Orchestre national de l’Opéra de Monte-Carlo, Louis Frémaux
intro: Altos and tenors begin a close pursuit through B minor; Bernard Kruysen answers them with the baritone’s Hostias. Fauré saves B major for the last “Amen”.

sections.label: A · Altos and tenors in canon
sections.mNote: The prayer begins again a step higher, then higher still

sections.label: B′ · Organ solo before Fac eas
sections.mNote: The organ sings between the baritone’s phrases

sections.label: A′ · Four voices take the canon
sections.mNote: The sopranos join the returning prayer

sections.label: Coda · Amen in B major
sections.mNote: Voices and organ finish after the strings fall silent

cues.title: Low strings climb
cues.text: Violas and cellos rise slowly above the organ, growing louder through the prelude. The marking is Adagio molto. Fauré leaves the violins, winds and harp out of this movement; the choir will sing among these low instruments.
cues.evidence: Hamelle full score (1901), pp. 23–44, especially the opening on pp. 23–24. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/4/4c/IMSLP30151-PMLP21398-Faure-Op048fs.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Two voices in pursuit
cues.text: Altos and tenors sing “O Domine Jesu Christe” in canon: one line follows closely behind the other. The narrow B minor tune begins pianissimo, marked dolcissimo. Each new appeal starts a step higher; the basses reinforce the later calls.
cues.evidence: Hamelle full score (1901), pp. 24–30: the altos’ and tenors’ canon, the rising statements and the basses’ later entries.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A prayer added later
cues.text: The baritone’s Hostias is completed in the spring of 1889, and the Libera me, written for voice and organ in 1877, joins the Requiem in 1891. On 21 January 1893 Fauré conducts the seven-movement work at the Madeleine, where he is choirmaster.
cues.evidence: Jean-Michel Nectoux, Harmonia Mundi HMM 931292 booklet note, https://www.harmoniamundi.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/12/931292_booklet.pdf (Hostias completed in the spring of 1889; Libera me written in 1877 for voice and organ and added in 1891; Fauré maître de chapelle of the parish). The performance of 21 January 1893 at the Madeleine: Wadham Sutton, Hyperion note, https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dw.asp?dc=W4018_68209

cues.title: An O that Fauré added
cues.text: The prayer is “O Domine Jesu Christe”, and the first word is Fauré’s own: the Offertory text begins at “Domine”. He also trims the words of the next verse and leaves out the third verse altogether.
cues.evidence: The text of the Offertory and Fauré’s changes: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Requiem_(Faur%C3%A9) (Text).

cues.title: Tired of funerals
cues.text: Fauré tells the interviewer Louis Aguettant in 1902 that, perhaps by instinct, he wanted to escape the conventional: “for so long I have been playing the organ at funeral services! I have had it up to here. I wanted to do something else.”
cues.evidence: Fauré to Louis Aguettant, 12 July 1902, published in Comœdia, 1954, p. 6; French text at http://www.rene-gagnaux.ch/inghelbrecht_desire-emile/faure_requiem.html (“voilà si longtemps que j’accompagne à l’orgue des services d’enterrement! J’en ai par-dessus la tête. J’ai voulu faire autre chose”). Translation ours.

cues.title: One voice offers Hostias
cues.text: The baritone begins “Hostias et preces” — offerings and prayers — on a repeated note. The pace is now Andante moderato, in three beats to the bar. Quiet quavers in the violas and cellos accompany him; the choir rests.
cues.evidence: Hamelle full score (1901), pp. 31–35: change to 3/4 and Andante moderato, baritone solo and repeated string quavers.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The baritone, Bernard Kruysen
cues.text: Bernard Kruysen, born in Montreux in 1933, was a Dutch baritone who studied in Paris with Pierre Bernac. He became one of the leading interpreters of French song, and Francis Poulenc accompanied him in recital.
cues.evidence: Grove Music biography of Kruysen (born 28 March 1933, Montreux; French government scholarship to study with Bernac; “recognized as one of the greatest interpreters” of French song in France; recitals with Poulenc), reproduced at https://www.bach-cantatas.com/Bio/Kruysen-Bernard.htm . The Erato sleeve credits him, “avec l’aimable autorisation des disques Valois”: https://archive.org/details/faure-o-requiem-cantique-de-jean-racine-louis-fremaux

cues.title: The organ answers alone
cues.text: The strings stop, and the organ has a small solo between the baritone’s phrases. He returns with “fac eas, Domine, de morte transire ad vitam”: let them pass from death to life. His melody moves more freely now.
cues.evidence: Hamelle full score (1901), pp. 36–38: organ marked Solo at F and the ensuing fac eas phrase.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The sopranos join the prayer
cues.text: The opening pace returns. This time all four choral parts take up the canon, including the sopranos who were silent at the start. Their entries overlap above the organ; the strings leave the voices room.
cues.evidence: Hamelle full score (1901), pp. 41–43: I° Tempo adagio molto and four-part choral imitation.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Religious illusion and eternal rest
cues.text: In 1921 Fauré wrote to René Fauchois that all the religious illusion he had ever had went into his Requiem, which is “dominated from one end to the other by a very human feeling: confidence in eternal rest”.
cues.evidence: Letter to René Fauchois, 1921 (dated 13 April 1921 on fr.wikipedia.org), quoted in French in the Orchestre Philharmonique Royal de Liège programme note by Éric Mairlot: « Tout ce que j’ai pu posséder d’illusion religieuse, je l’ai mise dans mon Requiem, lequel d’ailleurs est dominé d’un bout à l’autre par un sentiment bien humain : la confiance dans le repos éternel… », https://www.oprl.be/sites/default/files/2018-10/Requiem.pdf . English renderings differ: Jeremy Summerly, Hyperion CDA68209 booklet, https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dc.asp?dc=D_CDA68209 ; Michael Steinberg, Choral Masterworks (OUP, 2005), pp. 132–133 (not opened). The English here is ours, from the French.

cues.title: Amen turns to major
cues.text: Fauré adds “Amen” to the Offertory text. D♯ brightens the closing harmony into B major, and the voices pass the word between them. The strings sound one last chord, leaving the choir and organ to finish.
cues.evidence: Hamelle full score (1901), p. 44: change to five sharps and the final Amen. The addition to the text is documented at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Requiem_(Faur%C3%A9)
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Low strings make room for voices
transitions.to: A · Altos and tenors in canon
transitions.how: The rising viola and cello prelude diminishes. Altos and tenors begin the B minor canon pianissimo, marked dolcissimo, while the organ supports them. The melody passes from one choral part to the other in close succession.
transitions.evidence: Hamelle full score (1901), pp. 23–25: string prelude and the opening choral canon.

transitions.title: The baritone begins on one note
transitions.from: A · Altos and tenors in canon
transitions.how: The choir’s short phrases break off into rests. The baritone begins “Hostias” as the score changes to 3/4 and Andante moderato. D major opens beneath him; the violas and cellos repeat quiet quavers, and the organ is marked dolce.
transitions.evidence: Hamelle full score (1901), pp. 30–32: the end of the canon and the D major Hostias in 3/4.

transitions.title: The organ takes the next phrase
transitions.to: B′ · Organ solo before Fac eas
transitions.how: The strings release their chord at rehearsal F and the organ continues alone, marked Solo. Its upper line rises over a moving bass. The baritone returns on “fac eas” as the cellos rejoin, pianissimo; the triple metre continues unchanged.
transitions.evidence: Hamelle full score (1901), p. 36: organ solo at F, string rests and the baritone’s fac eas entry.

transitions.title: The slow canon returns
transitions.from: B′ · Organ solo before Fac eas
transitions.to: A′ · Four voices take the canon
transitions.how: The baritone finishes his promise of life. I° Tempo, adagio molto restores common time and B minor, and the choir begins “O Domine” again in overlapping entries. After one chord the strings rest, leaving the organ to accompany the four voices.
transitions.evidence: Hamelle full score (1901), pp. 40–41: the baritone’s close and the four-part return in common time.

transitions.title: B minor brightens to B major
transitions.from: A′ · Four voices take the canon
transitions.how: The last plea fades into “Amen”. D♯ replaces D♮ as the key signature changes from two sharps to five. The strings give the new B major chord one quiet stroke, then stop. Choir and organ continue the imitations to the final chord.
transitions.evidence: Hamelle full score (1901), pp. 43–44: Amen, B major and the withdrawal of the strings.

source.title: Fauré, Requiem, Op. 48, full orchestral score (Hamelle, 1901; Kalmus reprint)
source.locator: II. Offertoire, printed pp. 23–44: violas, cellos, double basses and organ accompany the choral canon and baritone Hostias. Voices and organ finish the Amen.

timeline.note: Violas and cellos rise together over the organ at Adagio molto.
Altos and tenors enter pianissimo in canon. The sopranos wait until the prayer returns.
The baritone sings “Hostias” over the violas’ and cellos’ repeated quavers.
At letter F, the organ takes a solo line. The strings fall back to occasional chords.
The choir returns with all four voices. Low strings and organ accompany the canon.
The choir begins “Amen”. One string chord marks the arrival in B major.
The voices finish their Amen with the organ alone.

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Bernard Kruysen (baritone), Chorale Philippe Caillard (chorus), Orchestre national de l’Opéra de Monte-Carlo (orchestra), Louis Frémaux (conductor), Henri Carol (organ)
fields.note: Commons lists Bernard Kruysen and Denis Thilliez among the artists of the complete recording; Kruysen is the baritone soloist here (the sleeve credits “Bernard Kruysen, baryton”). Denis Thilliez has no part in this movement.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Full-orchestra version, as published by Éditions Hamelle (1901)
fields.note: The sleeve credits “Editions Hamelle – Paris” and describes the version heard as the one with the more extended symphonic forces, which it says Fauré transcribed around 1899; Hamelle published the full-orchestra score in 1901. The sleeve names no editor or corrections, and the forces were not checked by ear against the score. Wikipedia notes that the 1900 autograph does not survive and that critics have asked who scored it, so authorship of the orchestration is not asserted here. The orchestra panel uses the Kalmus reprint of the Hamelle score.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: The scanned Erato sleeve prints “Enregistré … à Monaco, le 11 Août 1962”. The Commons date field (“10 August 1962”), IMSLP and René Gagnaux give 10 August 1962; Commons does not say whether its date is a session or an issue date. The 1988 CD reissue notes “Recording: 08/1962”. Both candidate days fall in 1962; the rights assessment relies on that year only.

fields.label: Place
fields.value: Cathedral of Our Lady Immaculate (Notre-Dame-de-l’Immaculée-Conception), Monaco
fields.note: The sleeve gives the cathedral in Monaco, and a 1983 Erato LP pressing (EF 28002) is noted on Discogs as “Registered in 1962 in the Cathedral of Monaco”. IMSLP and Gagnaux give the Salle Alcazar, Monte-Carlo. Commons gives no venue. The sleeve also credits the engineer: “Prise de son : Peter Willemoes”.
alts: Cathedral of Our Lady Immaculate (Notre-Dame-de-l’Immaculée-Conception), Monaco

fields.label: Label
fields.note: Commons names “Erato Records” as source; the sleeve, BnF and Discogs give the Erato label.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.note: The BnF notices list both issues with a 1962 legal-deposit date and cross-reference each other; the sleeve says the disc also exists in stereo as STE 50 128. Commons does not say which pressing, tape or CD its file derives from. The access MP3 is two-channel with a left/right correlation of 0.51 in this movement, so it is not a mono transfer, but that does not identify the carrier.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.note: No matrix or take numbers appear in the sources consulted. The sleeve lays out this movement as face 1, track 2 of the LP (face 1: Introït et Kyrie, Offertoire, Sanctus, Pie Jesu; face 2: Agnus Dei, Libera me, In paradisum, then the Cantique de Jean Racine).

fields.label: Transfer
fields.note: No transfer or restoration engineer is identified. Commons shows the file as uploaded by D. Benjamin Miller; an uploader is not assumed to be the engineer.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: The Commons upload date (23 May 2018) is not a transfer date.

fields.label: Processing
fields.note: No source-transfer or restoration processing is disclosed. Contrapunctus’ own analysis estimates the reference pitch of this movement about 40 to 60 cents above A = 440 Hz (+50 cents (CQT histogram) and −0.49 semitone (librosa estimate_tuning), the two figures being equivalent modulo a semitone); all seven movements of the set give a similar offset. Whether it comes from the orchestra’s tuning, the disc speed or the transfer speed is not established, and Hz and note names in the analysis report are not corrected for it.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Public domain in jurisdictions applying an unextended life-plus-70-year term
fields.note: Gabriel Fauré died in 1924. This assessment concerns the original composition, not a later edition, arrangement or this recording; it is not a worldwide rights clearance.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Territorial: sound recording in the public domain in the European Union (Commons PD-EU-audio; first published before 1963).
fields.note: Commons applies {{PD-EU-audio}} alone to this file (wikitext inspected at the cited revision; source “Erato Records”, date field 1962-08-10). The BnF catalogue records legal deposit in 1962 (“1962 (DL)”) for both Erato issues, LDE 3228 and STE 50128: that is the best primary evidence found that first publication came before 1963, so the 50-year EU term had expired before the term extension applied to recordings still protected on 1 November 2013 (Directive 2011/77/EU, Article 1(3)). Legal deposit is not an exact publication date and no issue month was found. The “℗ Erato Disques S.A. 1963” line on the 1988 CD reissue (ECD 40006) belongs to that reissue and is not taken as the date of first publication. A recording or session date is not used as a publication date. This is territorial and does not establish US sound-recording status.

composer.epithet: He spent his days at the organ and in the classroom, saving for songs and chamber music the harmonies nobody else could quite imagine.
facts: École Niedermeyer, 1854–65; Saint-Saëns became his teacher and lifelong friend
Songs, piano music, chamber music, Requiem and the opera Pénélope
composer.background:
The boy kept slipping into the chapel to play the harmonium. His father ran a teachers’ training school at Montgauzy, near Foix, and the little instrument in its chapel gave Gabriel Fauré his first musical happiness. In October 1854 his father took him to Paris and enrolled him at Louis Niedermeyer’s new school for church musicians. He was nine. For eleven years he lived among plainchant, organ exercises and the interweaving voices of Renaissance church music.

After Niedermeyer died in 1861, Camille Saint-Saëns took over the piano class. When the official lesson was done, he played the boys Schumann, Liszt and Wagner, composers far outside their syllabus. Fauré acquired a teacher, a champion and a friend who would stay beside him for sixty years. He left school in 1865 with prizes and the Cantique de Jean Racine: a French prayer unfolding over a flowing keyboard part, each new choral entry joining a phrase already under way.
